title: Installer partner rotation
subtitle: One local-logo campaign rolls in every 20 seconds while the left pane stays focused on the office setup.

items.title: Net30Hosting
items.summary: Hosting, email, domains, and managed infrastructure with business-credit-aware billing.
items.copy: Net30Hosting is the first offer to show during an install because every CreditSoft office needs a clean public lane before it starts onboarding clients. Use it for the domain, email, DNS, hosting, and managed infrastructure that support the website and portal side of the business. The pitch is simple: keep the credit repair operation local-first, but give the public brand professional hosting that can be invoiced on Net 30 terms. That makes the installer conversation easier during AnyDesk setup. While you configure the intranet node, the owner can open Net30Hosting, start the hosting account, pick the domain path, and keep the billing trail organized from day one. It is especially useful for new offices that need technical infrastructure, payment discipline, and a vendor relationship that reinforces the same business-credit habits they teach their own clients.
items.disclaimer: Logo is bundled locally for installer use; the button opens an external site.

items.title: Net30Brands
items.summary: Branding, website structure, and customer acquisition for offices that need the public face built with the install.
items.copy: Net30Brands belongs beside the installer because many offices do not just need software; they need a believable business front end. This lane is for the logo system, website copy, offer pages, lead capture, and conversion structure that make a credit repair company look ready before the first campaign goes live. The installer can keep CreditSoft local-first while Net30Brands handles the outside-facing presentation: homepage, pricing language, intake paths, calls to action, and the branded trust pieces that help prospects move from interest to booked consultation. It is a good second step after Net30Hosting because the domain and infrastructure are already being handled. During a remote setup, this ad gives the owner a direct place to think about brand, sales, and customer acquisition instead of burying those decisions inside technical install screens.
items.disclaimer: Bundled local artwork keeps the installer independent of remote image loads.

items.title: Tailscale
items.summary: Private tailnet access for staff devices, server nodes, MagicDNS names, and support sessions.
items.copy: Tailscale is the private access lane for the local-first CreditSoft model. The intranet should not need to sit wide open on the public internet just so staff can reach it from another device or so support can inspect a node. With Tailscale, the office can place the server, the owner laptop, support devices, and approved staff machines into a private tailnet. MagicDNS gives those machines friendly names, while the installer can still probe the node and guide the operator toward the correct local address. This makes the setup easier when the server is a Mac mini, Ryzen box, or office workstation sitting behind a normal router. The point of the ad is not to sell a cloud rewrite; it explains the private network layer that lets a local intranet behave like an office system even when support is remote.
items.disclaimer: Tailscale logo is cached in the installer assets; the button opens Tailscale externally.

items.title: ngrok
items.summary: Temporary HTTPS ingress for demos, webhooks, API callbacks, and support testing.
items.copy: ngrok is the controlled public lane for the moments when the local office needs to receive outside traffic without turning the whole intranet into a public website. During an install, that usually means testing webhook callbacks, showing a temporary demo, validating API behavior, or giving a support technician a short-lived route to a specific service. CreditSoft can stay local-first, and ngrok can provide a time-boxed HTTPS doorway when the workflow calls for one. The ad language should make that distinction clear: Tailscale is the private staff and support network; ngrok is the temporary public callback path. That keeps operators from confusing day-to-day intranet access with one-off external testing. It is also useful for companion plugin verification because the installer can explain why an outside service may need to talk back to the office node for a narrow setup step.
items.disclaimer: ngrok artwork is bundled locally so installer imagery does not depend on a CDN.

items.title: Google Drive
items.summary: Shared folders for document handoff, intake packets, exports, and office archive habits.
items.copy: Google Drive is the familiar document handoff lane for offices already living inside Google Workspace. It is not the database, not the intranet storage engine, and not the long-term replacement for a real backup plan. Its value is workflow: intake PDFs, client-uploaded paperwork, signed forms, exported packets, sales files, and shared folders that staff already understand. During an installer session, this ad reminds the operator to decide where outside documents land before the office starts taking clients. CreditSoft can still keep its casework and roster data in the local system, while Google Drive supports the human file-sharing layer around it. That separation matters. Staff get easy folders for daily work, the installer gets a clear backup destination choice, and the owner can keep client-facing document habits organized without asking every employee to learn server storage on day one.
items.disclaimer: Google Drive icon is bundled locally from existing CreditSoft installer assets.

items.title: Wasabi
items.summary: S3-compatible storage for snapshots, export archives, and off-machine backup retention.
items.copy: Wasabi is the storage lane for offices that want backups to land somewhere tougher than the same machine running the intranet. The installer can use it as the clean explanation for off-machine retention: database dumps, exported archives, branded site assets, generated packages, and recovery files can be pushed to S3-compatible storage on a schedule. This is different from a shared folder. Wasabi is for infrastructure-grade retention, not day-to-day staff collaboration. That distinction helps the owner understand why Google Drive and Dropbox can still be useful while a proper backup target remains necessary. In a local-first office, the server node is the primary system of record, so recovery planning matters. Wasabi gives the installer a simple place to point when the owner asks where snapshots should go after the box is configured and running.
items.disclaimer: Wasabi logo is copied into the local installer branding folder.

items.title: Dropbox
items.summary: Simple synced folders for offices that want a familiar staff handoff lane beside the intranet.
items.copy: Dropbox is the practical file-sync option for teams that want shared folders without building a full document process on day one. The installer can frame it as a companion lane: the intranet keeps the roster, cases, notes, billing signals, and office workflow; Dropbox can carry quick staff handoffs, import folders, export folders, review packets, and owner-accessible files that need to move between machines. For smaller offices, that familiarity matters. Staff may already know how to drag, drop, sync, and recover files without training. The ad should encourage a clean structure rather than a junk drawer: intake, disputes, signed authorizations, exports, archive, and temporary transfer. Used that way, Dropbox supports the local-first setup without pretending to be the database or the backup engine. The button uses the referral link requested for the installer campaign.
items.disclaimer: Dropbox logo is stored locally; the button opens the configured referral URL.

items.title: Amazon Hardware Pick
items.summary: A quick external buying lane for compact office server hardware when the client still needs a node.
items.copy: Some installs fail before software even starts because the office has no dependable machine to become the node. The Amazon hardware lane gives the operator a quick place to open a recommended compact box while the installer conversation is still fresh. CreditSoft does not need a giant server for every office; it needs a stable machine that can stay powered on, run Docker, hold the local intranet stack, reach the backup target, and join the private network. A small business desktop or mini workstation can be enough for many offices when storage, memory, and uptime expectations are chosen correctly. This ad helps during AnyDesk-style setup because the installer can say: if this laptop is temporary, buy a proper node and rerun the package there. It keeps the architecture honest: the office owns its infrastructure, and the intranet runs on a machine meant to stay in the office.
items.disclaimer: External Amazon link may use referral tracking. Installer image and logo are local assets.
